"Instead of burning or chopping up the prunings left over from winter garden maintenance, consider turning them into a dead hedge. This makes an excellent windbreak, provides shelter for birds and insects, and can also be used to separate different parts of your garden. To build one, place stakes or discarded fence posts in two parallel lines about 50cm apart, then pack the cut branches and twigs between them, using the thicker pieces at the bottom. The structure will compress and settle gradually as more material is added.  

If you want a gift for yourself, or were disappointed with what you received at Christmas, you could pre-order The Book of Seeds by Paul Smith, formerly the head of Kew’s Millennium Seed Bank. Due out in February and published by Ivy Press at £30, the book is a richly illustrated celebration of 600 of the strangest and most striking plant species on Earth, including a black seed with hair reminiscent of Donald Trump and tiny orchid seeds no bigger than a pinhead.  

For planting, winter-flowering clematis is especially rewarding. Given a warm, protected position in full sun, it can produce waves of flowers from December through February. Among the best choices are Clematis cirrhosa ‘Advent Bells’ and C. cirrhosa var. balearica, both of which bear creamy, fragrant blooms with maroon markings, as well as C. cirrhosa ‘Jingle Bells’, which flowers in pure white and can grow much larger. Is there anything else I can help with?"
